opus-5.5.text:
For me, the ultimate promise is giving the social sciences something they've never really had: a laboratory where you can actually run the experiment.

Think about how physics or biology advanced. A big part of it was the ability to build models, test interventions, and see what happens before you commit to something in the real world. The social sciences have always been constrained. If you want to know how a new policy will ripple through a community, or how misinformation spreads through a network, or how people will respond to a public health message, you mostly have to wait for it to happen, study it after the fact, or run small, expensive, slow studies with a limited number of participants. And you can never rerun history to see what would have happened if you'd done something differently.

What generative agents start to offer is the ability to create populations of simulated people, grounded in real human data, whose behavior is believable and, increasingly, measurably accurate, and then ask "what if?" What if we changed this policy? What if this rumor started in this part of the network instead of that one? You can run that a thousand times, vary the conditions, and look at the distribution of outcomes rather than a single anecdote.

I want to be careful here, because I don't think the goal is to replace studying real people. These simulations are only as good as their grounding, and we have a lot of work to do on validation: how closely an agent's responses track the actual person it's modeled on, where the simulations break down, where they reproduce biases. But if we get that right, I think we move from a world where we mostly explain social phenomena after the fact to one where we can reason about them prospectively. That's a huge shift, both for science and for how we make decisions as a society.

And there's a more personal dimension that excites me too. These tools let us ask deep questions about ourselves: what makes behavior human, what is consistent about a person across contexts, and what is context-dependent. Building agents that behave like us forces you to articulate those things precisely, and I think that's going to teach us a lot about human nature along the way.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the social sciences have always had this fundamental constraint, which is that you can't run the experiment twice. You can't take the same group of people, show them a policy, see how they react, then rewind and show them a different policy. So we've had to lean on surveys, on observational data, on small lab studies, and then make inferences from there. That's gotten us a long way, but it's a very indirect way of studying something as complex as human behavior.

What simulation offers, if we get it right, is something closer to what physics or biology have, which is a model you can poke at. You could ask, if we introduce this intervention into a community, what does the dynamic look like a month later? Not just for the average person, but for the whole range of people, with all their differences in background and values and the ways they influence each other. You could test a hundred variations of a public health message before any of them touches a real person. You could study phenomena like polarization or misinformation cascades in a setting where you can actually vary one thing at a time.

But I want to be careful here, because the promise is only real if the simulations are faithful. A simulation that's plausible but wrong is arguably worse than no simulation at all, because it gives you confidence you haven't earned. So a lot of the scientific work, to me, is in the validation. How do you know your simulated people behave like real people? Where do they diverge? And for which questions are they trustworthy and for which are they not? That's the part that turns this from a cool demo into a scientific instrument.

The other piece I care about is that the ultimate goal isn't to replace people. It's to build a better foundation for understanding each other. If you can represent the full diversity of how people think, not a flattened average, then the people designing systems and policies can see who they'd be leaving out before they build. That's where I think the real payoff is.

astra-6.text:
I think the ultimate promise is to give us a way to study how individual behavior produces collective outcomes. We make decisions as individuals, but those decisions interact, and out of that come things like norms, institutions, and social movements. Understanding that connection is incredibly difficult.

If we can build simulations that capture meaningful aspects of human behavior, we could use them to explore different explanations and ask counterfactual questions: What might change if we introduced a different policy or organized an institution differently? Those simulations wouldn’t replace studying real people. Their value would be in helping us develop better hypotheses and identify what we need to test in the real world.

So the scientific promise, to me, is a new experimental tool for understanding society—with the crucial caveat that we have to establish which behaviors these models capture and where they fail.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the ultimate promise is to help us understand how individual behavior gives rise to the collective world we live in. We make choices locally, interacting with a relatively small number of people, but out of those interactions emerge institutions, cultures, and social norms. Connecting those levels is a really difficult scientific problem.

If we can build simulations that meaningfully capture how people behave, we could use them to develop theories and explore interventions before trying them in the real world. What might happen if we change a policy? Who might benefit, and who might experience consequences we didn’t anticipate?

The important qualification is that a simulation is only useful to the extent that we can establish where it represents real people well and where it fails. So the promise isn’t a perfect digital society that tells us the future. It’s a new scientific instrument for asking better questions about society, generating hypotheses, and then testing those hypotheses against reality.
